U.S.-based Prolific participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that differed in thought-probe response options, which included or did not include "I-don't-know" and "mind-blanking" options in Study 1a, 1b, and 2 (Ns = 463-790).
Subjects were also confident and quick in their mind-blanking reports, with confidence ratings and report latencies matching other off-task thought categories.

Subjects completed hard or easy versions of the SART, or another sustained attention task (Seli et al., 2013), while responding to thought probes that included the following response options: 1) on task, 2) off task and I do remember what I was thinking about, 3) off-task but I do not remember what I was thinking about.

table.text: We conducted Study 1a using thought probes within the SART and replicated it in Study 1b using a longer SART to decrease on-task thought reports (and a larger participant sample to increase statistical power).
If mindblanking experiences are often miscategorized given the probe options, then mind-blanking rates should selectively drop when subjects are also offered an "I-don't-know" response.

table.text: Four hundred seventy-one subjects completed Study 1a and 786 completed Study 1b via the online recruitment site, Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/).
table.formatted: Four hundred seventy-one subjects completed Study 1a and 786 completed Study 1b via the online recruitment site, Prolific (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.co/">https://www.prolific.co</ref>).

table.text: Via Prolific prescreening, we limited the participating age range to 18-40 years, due to the decline in mind-wandering rates for older adults (e.g., Jackson & Balota, 2012; McVay et al., 2013); participant ages (after exclusions) for Studies 1a and 1b were M = 31.40, SD = 5.71, and M = 31.39, SD = 5.72, respectively.

table.text: Eligible subjects were compensated $4 (rate of $12/hr) for the 20-min study.
Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for any animal name and to withhold responses ("no-go") for any crop (fruit or vegetable) name; animal names occurred on 90% of the task trials.
Before the start of the task, subjects completed ten practice trials with boy names ("go") and girl names ("no-go").
For Study 1a, subjects completed 480 critical trials divided into four seamless blocks of 120 (16 unanalyzed buffer trials preceded the critical trials).
Each block also presented six thought probes to capture subjects' immediately preceding thoughts; these were randomized and then presented in the same order to everyone.

After the presentation of all probe options, subjects were reminded to choose the option that matched the content of their thoughts in the instant before the menu appeared and to use the numbers located at the top of the keyboard to respond to the probe.

After each thought report, subjects were asked to rate how confident they were Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 21 in their report by choosing a number on the keyboard on a number scale from 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (extremely confident).

As preregistered (https://osf.io/kxgqy/), to ensure that retained subjects were focused on the task, all data were dropped from subjects, case-wise, if: (a) they responded to fewer than 20 of the 24 probes in Study 1a, or to fewer than 30 of the 36 probes for Study 1b, before the 10 s probe-response deadline, or; (b) they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or; (c) they responded to any of the three media-multitasking questions with "Most of the time" or "All of the time."

table.text: We conducted pairwise comparisons via withinperson paired t-tests (with Holm corrections for multiple comparisons) to compare probe RTs between mind-blanking reports and those for other thought categories to examine whether subjects were especially slow to report mind-blanking.
Note that these RT analyses, here and across all our subsequent experiments, should be interpreted cautiously because many subjects had very few observations for each thought type.
We evaluated whether subjects were accepting or skeptical of mind-blanking experiences.
Most subjects were reportedly accepting of the mind-blanking phenomenon.

On one hand, these null results are surprising from the perspective that mind-blanking reports faithfully capture instances in which subjects were not experiencing the events around them (Ward & Wegner, 2013).

table.text: Online Prolific subjects may be highly motivated due to monetary rewards (and fearful of losing those rewards via inattentiveness), which may influence them to stay mentally on task at higher rates compared to typical laboratory subjects, and so additional efforts to decrease on-task thinking and boost overall mind-blanking rates seem warranted.

As a further attempt to decrease on-task experiences, we conducted Study 2 with a less demanding task because off-task thinking tends to increase with less demanding laboratory tasks (e.g., Matthews et al., 2024; Rummel & Boywitt, 2014; Seli et al., 2016).
table.formatted: As a further attempt to decrease on-task experiences, we conducted Study 2 with a less demanding task because off-task thinking tends to increase with less demanding laboratory tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Matthews et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rummel & Boywitt, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Seli et al., 2016)</ref>.

table.text: Study 2 administered a less demanding variation of the SART, which asked subjects to passively observe the word stimuli 90% of the time and respond only to the target category occurring 10% of the time, compared to the standard SART where subjects had to respond 90% of the time and inhibit responding 10% of the time.
Eight hundred and twenty U.S. Prolific subjects completed Study 2.
Subjects were paid $7.75 upon completion; by design, the full-study median completion time was about 35 min, which was 5 min longer than Study 1b, resulting in a pay rate of about $13/hr.
Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for the target category only, crops (fruits or vegetables), and to not press the spacebar ("don't-go") for animal names.
Subjects completed 10 practice trials with boy (no-go) and girl (go) names, ending with a thought probe according to the condition assignment.

Data from six subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three media-multitasking questions, or both.
Finally, although not preregistered (but consistent with Study 1a), data from two subjects were dropped because they somehow received more than 36 thought probes.

Unlike in Studies 1a and 1b, then, subjects were not significantly less confident in their mind-blanking reports than in their on-task reports, but of most importance, mind-blanking confidence was also at least as high as that for the other TUT categories, as it was in Studies 1a and 1b.
Very few subjects were skeptical of the phenomenon.
Subjects Before exclusions, 446 Prolific subjects completed Study 3.
Vigilance SART Subjects completed the same Vigilance SART as in Study 2, but with modified thought probes and instructions.
In this study, subjects were able to advance to the next instruction screen only after 3000 ms had elapsed (rather than 1500 ms previously).

Data from 7 subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three mediamultitasking questions, or both.
Confidence ratings for both unclear and absent reports were generally high in Study 3, suggesting that subjects were reasonably certain about both possible forms of mind-blanking.
Subjects were, moreover, highly confident in their mind-blanking reports in all three studies, and as confident as they were about content-laden TUT experiences.

Our provisional conclusions about the nature of mind-blanking and the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports, and our recommendations for future research, are based on four experimental studies conducted in an online attention-task context with Prolific participants living in the United States.

Mean rates of mind-blanking reports might have been higher in laboratory contexts, where there is less potential for environmental distractions, and with laboratory participants, who may be less concerned than Prolific participants that off-task thought reports might affect their compensation; other types of ongoing tasks, perhaps more Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 76 familiar ones affording automaticity of responding, might also yield higher reporting rates of mind-blanking and other off-task experiences.

In creative activities that might inspire flow, however, some participants might select a "mindblanking" thought-probe response option as closer to their subjective experience than is an "on task" option (e.g., Palhares et al., 2026). Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> U.S.-based Prolific participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that differed in thought-probe response options, which included or did not include "I-don't-know" and "mind-blanking" options in Study 1a, 1b, and 2 (Ns = 463-790).

> Subjects were also confident and quick in their mind-blanking reports, with confidence ratings and report latencies matching other off-task thought categories.

> Subjects completed hard or easy versions of the SART, or another sustained attention task (Seli et al., 2013), while responding to thought probes that included the following response options: 1) on task, 2) off task and I do remember what I was thinking about, 3) off-task but I do not remember what I was thinking about.

> We conducted Study 1a using thought probes within the SART and replicated it in Study 1b using a longer SART to decrease on-task thought reports (and a larger participant sample to increase statistical power).

> If mindblanking experiences are often miscategorized given the probe options, then mind-blanking rates should selectively drop when subjects are also offered an "I-don't-know" response.

> Four hundred seventy-one subjects completed Study 1a and 786 completed Study 1b via the online recruitment site, Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/).

> Via Prolific prescreening, we limited the participating age range to 18-40 years, due to the decline in mind-wandering rates for older adults (e.g., Jackson & Balota, 2012; McVay et al., 2013); participant ages (after exclusions) for Studies 1a and 1b were M = 31.40, SD = 5.71, and M = 31.39, SD = 5.72, respectively.

> Eligible subjects were compensated $4 (rate of $12/hr) for the 20-min study.

> Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for any animal name and to withhold responses ("no-go") for any crop (fruit or vegetable) name; animal names occurred on 90% of the task trials.

> Before the start of the task, subjects completed ten practice trials with boy names ("go") and girl names ("no-go").

> For Study 1a, subjects completed 480 critical trials divided into four seamless blocks of 120 (16 unanalyzed buffer trials preceded the critical trials).

> Each block also presented six thought probes to capture subjects' immediately preceding thoughts; these were randomized and then presented in the same order to everyone.

> After the presentation of all probe options, subjects were reminded to choose the option that matched the content of their thoughts in the instant before the menu appeared and to use the numbers located at the top of the keyboard to respond to the probe.

> After each thought report, subjects were asked to rate how confident they were Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 21 in their report by choosing a number on the keyboard on a number scale from 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (extremely confident).

> As preregistered (https://osf.io/kxgqy/), to ensure that retained subjects were focused on the task, all data were dropped from subjects, case-wise, if: (a) they responded to fewer than 20 of the 24 probes in Study 1a, or to fewer than 30 of the 36 probes for Study 1b, before the 10 s probe-response deadline, or; (b) they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or; (c) they responded to any of the three media-multitasking questions with "Most of the time" or "All of the time."

> As preregistered, data from three subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three media-multitasking questions, or both.

> We conducted pairwise comparisons via withinperson paired t-tests (with Holm corrections for multiple comparisons) to compare probe RTs between mind-blanking reports and those for other thought categories to examine whether subjects were especially slow to report mind-blanking.

> Note that these RT analyses, here and across all our subsequent experiments, should be interpreted cautiously because many subjects had very few observations for each thought type.

> We evaluated whether subjects were accepting or skeptical of mind-blanking experiences.

> Most subjects were reportedly accepting of the mind-blanking phenomenon.

> On one hand, these null results are surprising from the perspective that mind-blanking reports faithfully capture instances in which subjects were not experiencing the events around them (Ward & Wegner, 2013).

> Online Prolific subjects may be highly motivated due to monetary rewards (and fearful of losing those rewards via inattentiveness), which may influence them to stay mentally on task at higher rates compared to typical laboratory subjects, and so additional efforts to decrease on-task thinking and boost overall mind-blanking rates seem warranted.

> As a further attempt to decrease on-task experiences, we conducted Study 2 with a less demanding task because off-task thinking tends to increase with less demanding laboratory tasks (e.g., Matthews et al., 2024; Rummel & Boywitt, 2014; Seli et al., 2016).

> Study 2 administered a less demanding variation of the SART, which asked subjects to passively observe the word stimuli 90% of the time and respond only to the target category occurring 10% of the time, compared to the standard SART where subjects had to respond 90% of the time and inhibit responding 10% of the time.

> Eight hundred and twenty U.S. Prolific subjects completed Study 2.

> Subjects were paid $7.75 upon completion; by design, the full-study median completion time was about 35 min, which was 5 min longer than Study 1b, resulting in a pay rate of about $13/hr.

> Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for the target category only, crops (fruits or vegetables), and to not press the spacebar ("don't-go") for animal names.

> Subjects completed 10 practice trials with boy (no-go) and girl (go) names, ending with a thought probe according to the condition assignment.

> Data from six subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three media-multitasking questions, or both.

> Finally, although not preregistered (but consistent with Study 1a), data from two subjects were dropped because they somehow received more than 36 thought probes.

> Unlike in Studies 1a and 1b, then, subjects were not significantly less confident in their mind-blanking reports than in their on-task reports, but of most importance, mind-blanking confidence was also at least as high as that for the other TUT categories, as it was in Studies 1a and 1b.

> Very few subjects were skeptical of the phenomenon.

> Subjects Before exclusions, 446 Prolific subjects completed Study 3.

> Subjects were paid $7.75 upon completion.

> Vigilance SART Subjects completed the same Vigilance SART as in Study 2, but with modified thought probes and instructions.

> In this study, subjects were able to advance to the next instruction screen only after 3000 ms had elapsed (rather than 1500 ms previously).

> Data from 7 subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three mediamultitasking questions, or both.

> Confidence ratings for both unclear and absent reports were generally high in Study 3, suggesting that subjects were reasonably certain about both possible forms of mind-blanking.

> Subjects were, moreover, highly confident in their mind-blanking reports in all three studies, and as confident as they were about content-laden TUT experiences.

> Our provisional conclusions about the nature of mind-blanking and the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports, and our recommendations for future research, are based on four experimental studies conducted in an online attention-task context with Prolific participants living in the United States.

> Mean rates of mind-blanking reports might have been higher in laboratory contexts, where there is less potential for environmental distractions, and with laboratory participants, who may be less concerned than Prolific participants that off-task thought reports might affect their compensation; other types of ongoing tasks, perhaps more Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 76 familiar ones affording automaticity of responding, might also yield higher reporting rates of mind-blanking and other off-task experiences.

wandering. 1 In Experiment 1, subjects read chapters of War and Peace while responding to six thought probes with three response options: mind-wandering, mind-blanking, or mind-focused (i.e., on-task thought). Subjects reported mind-wandering more frequently than mind-blanking (M rates = .49 vs. .14, respectively). Mind-wandering and blanking rates also did not correlate significantly (r = -.06, N = 23), suggesting that these mental states might be phenomenologically distinct. Although the experiment was powered to detect only strong correlations, the metaanalytic estimate across their five experiments (with an appropriate sample size) was also nonsignificant and near zero, r = .03, N = 208. The apparent lack of correlation between probed mind-blanking and mind-wandering rates has also been replicated by others (r = .09, N = 292; Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024), supporting that these reports reflect dissociable phenomena.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1365 columns across 34 data files.
#### Issues Identified

249 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 34 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. live_data_statements: U.S.-based Prolific participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that differed in thought-probe response options, which included or did not include "I-don't-know" and "mind-blanking" options in Study 1a, 1b, and 2 (Ns = 463-790).
Subjects were also confident and quick in their mind-blanking reports, with confidence ratings and report latencies matching other off-task thought categories.

Subjects completed hard or easy versions of the SART, or another sustained attention task (Seli et al., 2013), while responding to thought probes that included the following response options: 1) on task, 2) off task and I do remember what I was thinking about, 3) off-task but I do not remember what I was thinking about.

We conducted Study 1a using thought probes within the SART and replicated it in Study 1b using a longer SART to decrease on-task thought reports (and a larger participant sample to increase statistical power).
If mindblanking experiences are often miscategorized given the probe options, then mind-blanking rates should selectively drop when subjects are also offered an "I-don't-know" response.
Four hundred seventy-one subjects completed Study 1a and 786 completed Study 1b via the online recruitment site, Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/).

Via Prolific prescreening, we limited the participating age range to 18-40 years, due to the decline in mind-wandering rates for older adults (e.g., Jackson & Balota, 2012; McVay et al., 2013); participant ages (after exclusions) for Studies 1a and 1b were M = 31.40, SD = 5.71, and M = 31.39, SD = 5.72, respectively.
Eligible subjects were compensated $4 (rate of $12/hr) for the 20-min study.
Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for any animal name and to withhold responses ("no-go") for any crop (fruit or vegetable) name; animal names occurred on 90% of the task trials.
Before the start of the task, subjects completed ten practice trials with boy names ("go") and girl names ("no-go").
For Study 1a, subjects completed 480 critical trials divided into four seamless blocks of 120 (16 unanalyzed buffer trials preceded the critical trials).
Each block also presented six thought probes to capture subjects' immediately preceding thoughts; these were randomized and then presented in the same order to everyone.

After the presentation of all probe options, subjects were reminded to choose the option that matched the content of their thoughts in the instant before the menu appeared and to use the numbers located at the top of the keyboard to respond to the probe.

After each thought report, subjects were asked to rate how confident they were Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 21 in their report by choosing a number on the keyboard on a number scale from 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (extremely confident).

As preregistered (https://osf.io/kxgqy/), to ensure that retained subjects were focused on the task, all data were dropped from subjects, case-wise, if: (a) they responded to fewer than 20 of the 24 probes in Study 1a, or to fewer than 30 of the 36 probes for Study 1b, before the 10 s probe-response deadline, or; (b) they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or; (c) they responded to any of the three media-multitasking questions with "Most of the time" or "All of the time."

As preregistered, data from three subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three media-multitasking questions, or both.

We conducted pairwise comparisons via withinperson paired t-tests (with Holm corrections for multiple comparisons) to compare probe RTs between mind-blanking reports and those for other thought categories to examine whether subjects were especially slow to report mind-blanking.
Note that these RT analyses, here and across all our subsequent experiments, should be interpreted cautiously because many subjects had very few observations for each thought type.
We evaluated whether subjects were accepting or skeptical of mind-blanking experiences.
Most subjects were reportedly accepting of the mind-blanking phenomenon.

On one hand, these null results are surprising from the perspective that mind-blanking reports faithfully capture instances in which subjects were not experiencing the events around them (Ward & Wegner, 2013).

Online Prolific subjects may be highly motivated due to monetary rewards (and fearful of losing those rewards via inattentiveness), which may influence them to stay mentally on task at higher rates compared to typical laboratory subjects, and so additional efforts to decrease on-task thinking and boost overall mind-blanking rates seem warranted.

As a further attempt to decrease on-task experiences, we conducted Study 2 with a less demanding task because off-task thinking tends to increase with less demanding laboratory tasks (e.g., Matthews et al., 2024; Rummel & Boywitt, 2014; Seli et al., 2016).

Study 2 administered a less demanding variation of the SART, which asked subjects to passively observe the word stimuli 90% of the time and respond only to the target category occurring 10% of the time, compared to the standard SART where subjects had to respond 90% of the time and inhibit responding 10% of the time.
Eight hundred and twenty U.S. Prolific subjects completed Study 2.
Subjects were paid $7.75 upon completion; by design, the full-study median completion time was about 35 min, which was 5 min longer than Study 1b, resulting in a pay rate of about $13/hr.
Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for the target category only, crops (fruits or vegetables), and to not press the spacebar ("don't-go") for animal names.
Subjects completed 10 practice trials with boy (no-go) and girl (go) names, ending with a thought probe according to the condition assignment.

Data from six subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three media-multitasking questions, or both.
Finally, although not preregistered (but consistent with Study 1a), data from two subjects were dropped because they somehow received more than 36 thought probes.

Unlike in Studies 1a and 1b, then, subjects were not significantly less confident in their mind-blanking reports than in their on-task reports, but of most importance, mind-blanking confidence was also at least as high as that for the other TUT categories, as it was in Studies 1a and 1b.
Very few subjects were skeptical of the phenomenon.
Subjects Before exclusions, 446 Prolific subjects completed Study 3.
Subjects were paid $7.75 upon completion.
Vigilance SART Subjects completed the same Vigilance SART as in Study 2, but with modified thought probes and instructions.
In this study, subjects were able to advance to the next instruction screen only after 3000 ms had elapsed (rather than 1500 ms previously).

Data from 7 subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three mediamultitasking questions, or both.
Confidence ratings for both unclear and absent reports were generally high in Study 3, suggesting that subjects were reasonably certain about both possible forms of mind-blanking.
Subjects were, moreover, highly confident in their mind-blanking reports in all three studies, and as confident as they were about content-laden TUT experiences.

Our provisional conclusions about the nature of mind-blanking and the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports, and our recommendations for future research, are based on four experimental studies conducted in an online attention-task context with Prolific participants living in the United States.

Mean rates of mind-blanking reports might have been higher in laboratory contexts, where there is less potential for environmental distractions, and with laboratory participants, who may be less concerned than Prolific participants that off-task thought reports might affect their compensation; other types of ongoing tasks, perhaps more Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 76 familiar ones affording automaticity of responding, might also yield higher reporting rates of mind-blanking and other off-task experiences.

In creative activities that might inspire flow, however, some participants might select a "mindblanking" thought-probe response option as closer to their subjective experience than is an "on task" option (e.g., Palhares et al., 2026). (Kawagoe et al., 2018; 2019; 2024), as well as in Europe (e.g., Boulakis et al., 2023; Koroma et al., 2023; Mortaheb et al., 2022) and North America (e.g., Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024; Ward & Wegner, 2013), this represents a limited participant pool to establish the validity of a fascinating and potentially underappreciated state of consciousness.

Mind-blanking reports: (a) did not decrease when participants were provided with a thought-probe option to indicate that they could not remember their preceding thoughts; (b) elicited confidence ratings that were numerically and categorically high (averaging between 3.5-4 on a 5-point scale, between the scale labels, "confident" and "very confident"), similar to those elicited by content-laden TUT reports, and; (c) were made with similar latencies as content-laden TUT reports.

If we are wrong, however, and mind-blanking reports did primarily reflect I-don't-know experiences that participants mischaracterized, then all of the following would need to be true: (a) participants chose not to use the available "I-don't-know" response option to report these experiences, despite prior mind-wandering research indicating that participants are quite willing to report such memory failures (Mathews et al., 2024; Yeo et al., 2026); (b) participants chose to report high confidence in their mind-blanking reports despite their not actually remembering what they had experienced, and; (c) the response threshold for failing to recall one's experience and then making an attribution (i.e., to indicate a negative/"absence") is no higher-and its response latency is no longer-than that for recalling and reporting one's experience (i.e., to indicate a positive/"presence"), despite all three of our studies showing (non-significantly) longer report latencies-by 400 to 1400 ms-for I-don't-know reports than for mind-blanking reports.
Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

The consent form to participate indicated that this was a research study and that there would be "written reports" of the research, although it did not specify publication in a scientific journal; as well, participants were informed that their de-identified data would be posted to an online repository for other scientists to access.

Figure 2: Frequency distributions and box plots for on-task, daydream, mind-blanking (MB), but no IDK condition compared to the MB & IDK condition, providing evidence that subjects were mis-categorizing I-don't-know experiences as mind-blanking reports.

Similarly, a DES-related study of adults with hippocampal damage (n = 6) versus healthy controls (n = 12), conducted in a lab setting while subjects were in "restful moments," found that subjects in both groups sometimes spontaneously reported having no thoughts, or a blank mind, when probed (M frequency = 0.4 times for controls, 1.8 for patients;McCormick et al., 2018).

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 8 scripts: 0 ran without error, 5 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **3 scripts need the internet**, which is off during the run: Validity of Mind Blanking Reports Study 2 Vigilance SART.Rmd, Validity of Mind Blanking Reports Study 2.Rmd, Validity of Mind Blanking Reports.Rmd. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this. **A script looked for a file in another folder than the deposit has it**, so before running it once more we copied it there: `Study 2/Raw Data/ContentBlank.csv` to `Study 3/Raw data/ContentBlank.csv` for `Study3-Validity-of-Mind-Blanking-Reports-Vigilance-SART.Rmd`. info.title: Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 1 What Is a "Blank" Mind? Testing the Meaning and Construct Validity of Mind-Blanking Reports to Thought Probes
keywords: construct validity Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 3

author.affiliation: Washington University in St. Louis Michael J. Kane

Department of Psychology
								UNC Greensboro
								
									P.O. Box 26170
									27402- 6170
									Greensboro
									NC

text.text: Four studies evaluated probed mind-blanking reports, an off-task conscious state ostensibly experienced as an absence of thought and subjective experience.

We examined whether people make mind-blanking reports to indicate uncertainty about their preceding thoughts, rather than to communicate an experienced "blank;" we also assessed whether subjects used "blank" to refer to the absence of experience, or rather an unclear, diffuse form of experience.

U.S.-based Prolific participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that differed in thought-probe response options, which included or did not include "I-don't-know" and "mind-blanking" options in Study 1a, 1b, and 2 (Ns = 463-790).
Within an online go/no-go task, we tested whether different response options yielded different rates of mind-blanking and I-don't-know reports.
That is, would mind-blanking rates be higher when an "I don't know" response option was not available, suggesting that mind-blanking reports indicate uncertainty?
Would rates of Idon't-know reports be lower when the "mind-blanking" option was unavailable?
Neither mindblanking nor I-don't-know report rates differed significantly between probe-type conditions.
Subjects were also confident and quick in their mind-blanking reports, with confidence ratings and report latencies matching other off-task thought categories.
Subjects didn't use mindblanking reports to reflect uncertainty.

Study 3 (N = 415) extended our construct-validity investigation to the phenomenology of mind-blanking by separating (within subjects) "mindblanking" response options into "unclear or foggy thoughts" versus "complete absence of experience."
Unclear thoughts accounted for 3% of thought reports, versus 1% reflecting no experience, suggesting that "blanking" more often reflects diffuse than absent subjective states.
wandering.
1 In Experiment 1, subjects read chapters of War and Peace while responding to six thought probes with three response options: mind-wandering, mind-blanking, or mind-focused (i.e., on-task thought).
Subjects reported mind-wandering more frequently than mind-blanking (M rates = .49 vs. .14, respectively).
Mind-wandering and blanking rates also did not correlate significantly (r = -.06, N = 23), suggesting that these mental states might be phenomenologically distinct.

Although the experiment was powered to detect only strong correlations, the metaanalytic estimate across their five experiments (with an appropriate sample size) was also nonsignificant and near zero, r = .03, N = 208.

The apparent lack of correlation between probed mind-blanking and mind-wandering rates has also been replicated by others (r = .09, N = 292; Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024), supporting that these reports reflect dissociable phenomena.

text.text: The apparent distinction between mind-blanking and mind-wandering was reinforced by additional experiments by Ward and Wegner (2013) correlating thought-report rates with performance scores on reading comprehension tests.
text.formatted: The apparent distinction between mind-blanking and mind-wandering was reinforced by additional experiments by <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Ward and Wegner (2013)</ref> correlating thought-report rates with performance scores on reading comprehension tests.

text.text: In three experiments (Ns = 27-75), in which subjects self-caught their mind-blanking and mind-wandering episodes during a self-paced reading task, mind-wandering report counts correlated negatively with comprehension scores (rs ≈ -.40).

Watts and Sharrock (1985) had depressed patients catch themselves whenever they lost concentration during a reading task and then indicate whether they were thinking about something else; for 19% of lapses, subjects indicated they weren't thinking about something else, suggestive of mindblanking (these patients also reported in clinical interviews that blanking was a less frequent concentration problem in everyday life than was mind-wandering). text.text: Finally, Jackson and Balota (2012) conducted a study of aging and mind-wandering that included a thought-probe response option to report mind-blanking ("space outs"); older adults reported fewer mindblanking and mind-wandering experiences than did younger adults (subsequent findings suggested that mind-blanking does not differ significantly between healthy older adults and those with Alzheimers disease (Gyurkovics et al., 2018) or between older adults showing cognitive stability and those showing cognitive decline (Welhaf et al., 2025).

text.text: remembered less about what they read.
Mind-blanking counts, in contrast, were uncorrelated with reading comprehension across experiments (rs ≈ .00), suggesting different downstream consequences.

Both mind-blanking and mind-wandering counts correlated negatively with comprehension scores only when subjects read on-screen with the pace controlled by the computer, rather than by the subject (rs ≈ -.35).

These reading findings suggested that, during mind-wandering, people may lack meta-awareness of their disconnect from their task and surroundings and thus fail to stop advancing the screens that they haven't effectively read.

During mind-blanking, however, subjects may have gone beyond "autopilot" and stopped altogether moving their eyes across the screen and pressing keys to advance to the next paragraph, thus allowing them to recover when their thoughts returned to the self-paced text.

The lack of correlation between mind-blanking and mind-wandering rates, and their divergent correlations with comprehension of self-paced reading, provide evidence for the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports, insofar as they reflect subjects distinguishing the experiences of content-absent from content-laden off-task thought.

Below, we first consider other positive evidence for construct validity in the literature, which similarly indicates some distinctions between mind-blanking and mind-wandering (and on-task thought) reports.
We then discuss other evidence that may be more problematic for claims of validity.
Several lines of behavioral evidence provisionally suggest that probed mind-blanking reports may be valid.

In multiple samples, mind-blanking propensity has been more strongly related to ADHD symptoms than is mind-wandering during laboratory attention tasks (such as the go/no-go "Sustained Attention to Response Task" [SART]; Robertson et al., 1997).
text.formatted: In multiple samples, mind-blanking propensity has been more strongly related to ADHD symptoms than is mind-wandering during laboratory attention tasks (such as the go/no-go "Sustained Attention to Response Task" <ref type="bibr">[SART]</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Robertson et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: In Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 7 undergraduates, rates of mind-blanking correlated significantly with self-reported ADHD symptoms whereas rates of mind-wandering did not (Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024).
text.formatted: In Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 7 undergraduates, rates of mind-blanking correlated significantly with self-reported ADHD symptoms whereas rates of mind-wandering did not <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Further, in adults assessed for ADHD via diagnostic interview, those high in ADHD symptomology (n = 15) had higher mind-blanking rates, but not mind-wandering rates, than did those low in ADHD symptomology (n = 25; Van den Driessche et al., 2017, Study 2).
text.formatted: Further, in adults assessed for ADHD via diagnostic interview, those high in ADHD symptomology (n = 15) had higher mind-blanking rates, but not mind-wandering rates, than did those low in ADHD symptomology (n = 25; <ref type="bibr">Van den Driessche et al., 2017, Study 2)</ref>.

text.text: In children aged 6-12, the findings are more complex (perhaps suggestive of self-report challenges with young children): Those with untreated ADHD showed higher mind-blanking rates than those with pharmacologically treated ADHD and healthy and clinical controls (ns = 19-20 in each group), but those with treated ADHD showed higher mind-wandering rates than did those with untreated ADHD and controls (Van den Driessche et al., 2017, Study 1).
text.formatted: In children aged 6-12, the findings are more complex (perhaps suggestive of self-report challenges with young children): Those with untreated ADHD showed higher mind-blanking rates than those with pharmacologically treated ADHD and healthy and clinical controls (ns = 19-20 in each group), but those with treated ADHD showed higher mind-wandering rates than did those with untreated ADHD and controls <ref type="bibr">(Van den Driessche et al., 2017, Study 1)</ref>.

text.text: Only one study that we're aware of, in adults, found that a diagnosed ADHD group showed both more mind-blanking and more mind-wandering during the SART than did controls (Madiouni et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Only one study that we're aware of, in adults, found that a diagnosed ADHD group showed both more mind-blanking and more mind-wandering during the SART than did controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Madiouni et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: More limited evidence suggests that mind-blanking and mind-wandering may also be differentially associated with in-the-moment SART performance.

Specifically, mind-blanking reports were immediately preceded by more "go" trial misses than were mind-wandering reports (with both preceded by more misses than were on-task thought reports; Andrillon et al., 2021;   Munoz-Musat et al., 2025 2 ), and mind-blanking was preceded by go-trial sequences with longer RTs than was mind-wandering (Andrillon et al., 2021; Munoz-Musat et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Specifically, mind-blanking reports were immediately preceded by more "go" trial misses than were mind-wandering reports (with both preceded by more misses than were on-task thought reports; Andrillon et al., 2021;   Munoz-Musat et al., 2025 2 ), and mind-blanking was preceded by go-trial sequences with longer RTs than was mind-wandering <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andrillon et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Munoz-Musat et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Such findings might indicate that mind-blanking is associated with a more complete withdrawal of external processing than is mind-wandering.

Evidence also suggests, however, that mind-blanking and mind-wandering reports are preceded by similar false-alarm ("no go") error rates (Andrillon et al., 2021; Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024; Munoz-Musat et al., 2025), and by similar RT variability over the preceding four go-task trials (Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024).
text.formatted: Evidence also suggests, however, that mind-blanking and mind-wandering reports are preceded by similar false-alarm ("no go") error rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andrillon et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Munoz-Musat et al., 2025)</ref>, and by similar RT variability over the preceding four go-task trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We note that these positive findings were not, as far as we're aware, predicted by theory.

There doesn't seem to be a compelling or coherent explanation for why mind-blanking and mind-wandering propensities might be differentially related to medicated versus unmedicated ADHD in children, or why mind-blanking should be more strongly associated with ADHD symptoms in adults than is mind-wandering, or why mind-blanking might be more strongly associated with target misses and mean RTs than is mind-wandering, but not with other performance indicators like false alarms or RT variability.

From the nomothetic span approach to construct validity, however, which relies on patterns of associations versus dissociations among measures of similar versus dissimilar constructs (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Embretson, 1983), finding any replicable differences between mind-blanking and mind-wandering suggests that people's self-reports are reflecting distinctions of some kind between these experiences.
text.formatted: From the nomothetic span approach to construct validity, however, which relies on patterns of associations versus dissociations among measures of similar versus dissimilar constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cronbach & Meehl, 1955;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Embretson, 1983)</ref>, finding any replicable differences between mind-blanking and mind-wandering suggests that people's self-reports are reflecting distinctions of some kind between these experiences.

text.text: The validity of mind-blanking reports is also partially supported by fMRI findings, but evidence is mixed.

During attempts to "think of nothing" with occasional thought probes, periods preceding mind-blanking reports showed deactivation in Broca's area and left anterior insula relative to mind-wandering periods, but only with a liberal post-hoc significance threshold and not with planned conservative thresholds (Kawagoe et al., 2019).
text.formatted: During attempts to "think of nothing" with occasional thought probes, periods preceding mind-blanking reports showed deactivation in Broca's area and left anterior insula relative to mind-wandering periods, but only with a liberal post-hoc significance threshold and not with planned conservative thresholds <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kawagoe et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, during rest, regionof-interest analyses found deactivations preceding mind-blanking versus mind-wandering reports in ventromedial PFC/anterior cingulate cortex, but no differences in Broca's area (Boulakis et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Moreover, during rest, regionof-interest analyses found deactivations preceding mind-blanking versus mind-wandering reports in ventromedial PFC/anterior cingulate cortex, but no differences in Broca's area <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boulakis et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than focusing on a priori regions of interest, connectivity analyses during rest indicated greater global signal amplitude preceding mind-blanking reports versus mind-wandering reports, and periods preceding mind-blanking reports consistently showed a connectivity pattern like that associated with slow-wave sleep (Mortaheb et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Rather than focusing on a priori regions of interest, connectivity analyses during rest indicated greater global signal amplitude preceding mind-blanking reports versus mind-wandering reports, and periods preceding mind-blanking reports consistently showed a connectivity pattern like that associated with slow-wave sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Mortaheb et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, EEG findings from three thought-probe studies may also (provisionally) imply construct validity of mind-blanking reports.

During the SART, mind-blanking periods produced slow wave signatures more similar to sleep than did mind-wandering (Andrillon et al., 2021; Munoz-Musat et al., 2025), and mind-blanking was characterized by an absence of late processing (i.e., virtually absent P3b component) in contrast to mind-wandering and on-task thought (Munoz-Musat et al., 2025).
text.formatted: During the SART, mind-blanking periods produced slow wave signatures more similar to sleep than did mind-wandering <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andrillon et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Munoz-Musat et al., 2025)</ref>, and mind-blanking was characterized by an absence of late processing (i.e., virtually absent P3b component) in contrast to mind-wandering and on-task thought <ref type="bibr">(Munoz-Musat et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: During rest, balanced random forest classifiers based on EEG, electrocardiogram, pupillometry, and electrodermal data taken before each thought probe achieved above-chance accuracy in classifying mind-blanking periods versus other off-task thought periods in known subjects, but no classifier successfully did so in out-of-sample subjects (Boulakis et al., 2025).
text.formatted: During rest, balanced random forest classifiers based on EEG, electrocardiogram, pupillometry, and electrodermal data taken before each thought probe achieved above-chance accuracy in classifying mind-blanking periods versus other off-task thought periods in known subjects, but no classifier successfully did so in out-of-sample subjects <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Boulakis et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Many of the neuroscience results described above are suggestive, particularly those associating mind-blanking reports with sleep-like slow waves.
Such findings are helpful to establishing construct validity, by linking mind-blanking self-reports with more "objective" indicators of experience.

But given some inconsistencies in findings across and within studies (such as those for Broca's area), the small samples (Ns < 40), and the lack of independent replications so far, more consistent and robust evidence will be needed from future neuroscience studies to compellingly support the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports.

text.text: Some findings suggest skepticism is warranted about mind-blanking reports. Ward and Wegner (2013, Experiments 2a and 3a) used the self-catch method (Schooler et al., 2004) to capture off-task experiences during reading.
text.formatted: Some findings suggest skepticism is warranted about mind-blanking reports. <ref type="bibr">Ward and Wegner (2013, Experiments 2a and 3a)</ref> used the self-catch method <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Schooler et al., 2004)</ref> to capture off-task experiences during reading.

text.text: Subjects pressed a button whenever they spontaneously realized they were off-task; they had to then indicate whether they had been mindwandering or mind-blanking, followed by a dichotomous question to confirm or disconfirm their reports ("Are you sure?").
Mind-wandering reports were more frequent than mind-blanking reports, but most relevant here is the percentage of corrections made for both mental states.
Of the total mind-blanking reports in Experiments 2a and 3a, respectively, 81% and 86% were confirmed, compared to 97% and 96% confirmed mind-wandering reports.
Initial mind-blanking reports were corrected considerably more often than mind-wandering reports, which were confirmed nearly every time.
Mind-blanking reports, then, although frequently confirmed, were made with less certainty than mind-wandering reports.
We see further evidence for an apparent hesitation around mind-blanking reports in Kawagoe et al. (2019).
text.formatted: We see further evidence for an apparent hesitation around mind-blanking reports in <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kawagoe et al. (2019)</ref>.

text.text: Here, subjects tried to think of nothing during an fMRI scan and respond to occasional thought probes.
When subjects made a mind-blanking report, they were asked whether they were truly mind-blanking or just trying to follow the instructions.
Overall, subjects reported mind-blanking to 57% of the probes.
The follow-up confirmation question reduced the rate dramatically, to 32%.
The sharp decline in mind-blanking reports after double-checking once again indicates uncertainty around mind-blanking experiences.

One explanation for low confidence in mind-blanking reports is the difficulty that subjects might face in recalling their thoughts, especially considering that people often mindwander without awareness until they are interrupted by a probe (e.g., Schooler et al. 2004; Smallwood et al., 2008).
text.formatted: One explanation for low confidence in mind-blanking reports is the difficulty that subjects might face in recalling their thoughts, especially considering that people often mindwander without awareness until they are interrupted by a probe (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Schooler et al. 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Smallwood et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, Mathews et al. (2024) provided evidence that people can nearly immediately forget their off-task thought content.
text.formatted: In fact, <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Mathews et al. (2024)</ref> provided evidence that people can nearly immediately forget their off-task thought content.

text.text: Subjects completed hard or easy versions of the SART, or another sustained attention task (Seli et al., 2013), while responding to thought probes that included the following response options: 1) on task, 2) off task and I do remember what I was thinking about, 3) off-task but I do not remember what I was thinking about.

text.text: Subjects frequently reported being off task but unable to remember what they were thinking about (Ms ≈ 15-20% of all responses; see also Yeo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Subjects frequently reported being off task but unable to remember what they were thinking about (Ms ≈ 15-20% of all responses; see also <ref type="bibr">Yeo et al., 2025</ref>).

text.text: An occasional lack of meta-awareness during mind-wandering episodes may disrupt the subsequent recall of off-task thought content.
In such instances of not knowing what one was thinking, or "drawing a blank" in recollection, the uncertainty about experience might be perceived by subjects as mind-blanking (Mathews et al. 2024).
text.formatted: In such instances of not knowing what one was thinking, or "drawing a blank" in recollection, the uncertainty about experience might be perceived by subjects as mind-blanking <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Mathews et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This might be especially likely if thought probes provide an option to report mind-blanking but not to report uncertainty or a failure to recall.

That is, the inability to produce or access information (as in the tip-of-thetongue phenomenon), or the unawareness of what one was just thinking about, may lead some subjects to mistakenly report their prior experience as mind-blanking.
Reporting conscious experiences is constrained by the response options available, which may skew the findings and conclusions (see, e.g., Fell, 2022; Kane et al., 2021; Weinstein, 2018).
text.formatted: Reporting conscious experiences is constrained by the response options available, which may skew the findings and conclusions (see, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fell, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kane et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Weinstein, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: If probed mind-blanking studies do not provide response options to decipher between I-don't-know responses and other mental content (or lack thereof), then we cannot be confident that subjects truly experienced mind-blanking.

It may be surprising that few published mind-blanking studies have offered a "don't remember" response option on thought probes, especially considering the ambiguity surrounding self-reports and the mind-blanking phenomenon. Andrillion et al. (2021) and Munoz-Masat et al., 2025 found that 1.1% and 2.6%, respectively, of all probes elicited responses of "don't remember," which were then combined with mind-blanking reports as "mind-blanking" rates by the investigators (Corcoran et al., 2025, and Palhares et al., 2026, also combined these response options in "mind blanking" rates without reporting them separately).

(2021)</ref> and Munoz-Masat et al., 2025 found that 1.1% and 2.6%, respectively, of all probes elicited responses of "don't remember," which were then combined with mind-blanking reports as "mind-blanking" rates by the investigators <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Corcoran et al., 2025, and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Palhares et al., 2026</ref>, also combined these response options in "mind blanking" rates without reporting them separately).

text.text: We suggest that these two options should not be used interchangeably.

Relatedly, some mind-wandering studies have combined mind-blanking with other mental states within the same response option in their thought probes ("I am not very alert/My mind is blank"; e.g., Robison et al., 2018 Robison et al., , 2022;; Robison & Unsworth, 2018; Unsworth & Robison, 2018).
text.formatted: Relatedly, some mind-wandering studies have combined mind-blanking with other mental states within the same response option in their thought probes ("I am not very alert/My mind is blank"; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Robison et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Robison et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Robison & Unsworth, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Unsworth & Robison, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: If the field is interested in better understanding the mind-blanking phenomenon, it must do a better job of conceptualizing and measuring it.

Despite growing scientific interest in mind-blanking experiences (for reviews, see Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Kaufmann et al., 2024), researchers have yet to rigorously test the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports.
text.formatted: Despite growing scientific interest in mind-blanking experiences (for reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kaufmann et al., 2024)</ref>, researchers have yet to rigorously test the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports.

text.text: This is concerning, considering the possibility that mind-blanking reports may reflect uncertainty or a lack of awareness of one's thoughts, rather than a true experience of nothingness, leading to possibly erroneous conclusions about mind-blanking phenomena (for related concerns, see Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Fell, 2022).
text.formatted: This is concerning, considering the possibility that mind-blanking reports may reflect uncertainty or a lack of awareness of one's thoughts, rather than a true experience of nothingness, leading to possibly erroneous conclusions about mind-blanking phenomena (for related concerns, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fell, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The present study, therefore, assessed the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports in four online asynchronous studies.

Specifically, we tested whether mind-blanking experiences are reported consistently across different varieties of thought probes, some of which allowed subjects to indicate a lack of certainty about their preceding conscious state.

We conducted Study 1a using thought probes within the SART and replicated it in Study 1b using a longer SART to decrease on-task thought reports (and a larger participant sample to increase statistical power).

We then conducted Study 2 using an easier "vigilance" version of the SART and increased the duration of the stimuli to reduce the task demands, reduce on-task thoughts, and increase reporting of off-task thoughts.

Finally, Study 3 was conducted to investigate further what the "blank" in mind-blanking may have meant to subjects; that is, did subjects use mind-blanking to refer to a complete lack of experience, or rather a lack of clear and specific thoughts but with some subjective experience (Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Fell, 2022)?
text.formatted: Finally, Study 3 was conducted to investigate further what the "blank" in mind-blanking may have meant to subjects; that is, did subjects use mind-blanking to refer to a complete lack of experience, or rather a lack of clear and specific thoughts but with some subjective experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fell, 2022)</ref>?

text.text: Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 all tested whether probes that differed in response options would yield significantly different rates of mind-blanking and I-don't-know reports.
Specifically, these between-subject studies presented subjects with one of three different thought probes during the SART.
An "I-don't-know" option was provided to distinguish between I-don't-know and mind-
Rates of mind-blanking were compared between this MB & IDK condition and a condition including only a "mind-blanking" option (MB but no IDK condition).

text.text: Additionally, rates of Idon't-know reports were compared between conditions that either included only the "I-don'tknow" response option (IDK but no MB condition) or both relevant options (MB & IDK condition).
text.formatted: Additionally, rates of Idon't-know reports were compared between conditions that either included only the "I-don'tknow" response option (IDK but no MB condition) or both relevant options (MB & IDK condition).

text.text: Our reasoning was that, if subjects sometimes inaccurately report experiences of mindblanking because they forgot or were unsure of their previous thoughts (Mathews et al., 2024), then rates of mind-blanking and I-don't-know responses should differ systematically across conditions that vary in including "I-don't-know" and "mind-blanking" response options.
text.formatted: Our reasoning was that, if subjects sometimes inaccurately report experiences of mindblanking because they forgot or were unsure of their previous thoughts <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Mathews et al., 2024)</ref>, then rates of mind-blanking and I-don't-know responses should differ systematically across conditions that vary in including "I-don't-know" and "mind-blanking" response options.

text.text: If mindblanking experiences are often miscategorized given the probe options, then mind-blanking rates should selectively drop when subjects are also offered an "I-don't-know" response.

Since there were response options to distinguish between I-don't-know and mind-blanking experiences in the MB & IDK condition, we expected rates of mind-blanking to be lower in this condition compared to the one that only provided the "mind-blanking" but no "I-don't-know" response option.
text.formatted: Since there were response options to distinguish between I-don't-know and mind-blanking experiences in the MB & IDK condition, we expected rates of mind-blanking to be lower in this condition compared to the one that only provided the "mind-blanking" but no "I-don't-know" response option.

text.text: Moreover, if some mind-blanking reports arise from I-don't-know experiences, then this should also selectively increase I-don't-know report rates in the condition without the "mindblanking" option (IDK but no MB condition): Reports that would have been miscategorized as blanking should now be accurately reported, resulting in higher rates of I-don't-know reports.

In comparison, subjects in the MB & IDK condition should produce lower rates of I-don't-know reports compared to subjects in the IDK but no MB condition due to the possibility of reporting Idon't-know experiences as blanking in the former.
text.formatted: In comparison, subjects in the MB & IDK condition should produce lower rates of I-don't-know reports compared to subjects in the IDK but no MB condition due to the possibility of reporting Idon't-know experiences as blanking in the former.

text.text: In prior studies (Kawagoe et al. 2019; Ward & Wegner, 2013), mind-blanking reports have been corrected more often than mind-wandering reports, suggesting ambiguity associated with the experience of mind-blanking.
text.formatted: In prior studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kawagoe et al. 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Ward & Wegner, 2013)</ref>, mind-blanking reports have been corrected more often than mind-wandering reports, suggesting ambiguity associated with the experience of mind-blanking.

text.text: Accordingly, we administered confidence ratings after each thought report in the MB but no IDK condition in Experiments 1a, 1b, and 2, and predicted that confidence in mind-blanking reports would be lower than for other off-task thought reports.

Finally, as argued above, a lack of clarity about an immediately preceding conscious experience (i.e., uncertain or inaccessible thoughts) might result in subjects defaulting to reporting mind-blanking, even if they had not actually been devoid of conscious experience (Mathews et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Finally, as argued above, a lack of clarity about an immediately preceding conscious experience (i.e., uncertain or inaccessible thoughts) might result in subjects defaulting to reporting mind-blanking, even if they had not actually been devoid of conscious experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Mathews et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: If some mind-blanking reports derive from uncertainty rather than a true "blanking" of consciousness, then subjects might take more time to report mind-blanking than other off-task experiences because they are searching for content or waiting for necessary information to accumulate.
The same should be true for "don't know" responses, as subjects must engage in a search process if the preceding thoughts or experience do not immediately come to mind.
Thus, we hypothesized that mind-blanking RTs and I-don't-know RTs would be similar, with both significantly longer than those for other thought category reports.
To preview, the findings from Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 indicated that mind-blanking reports were not simply mislabeled reports of being unsure about one's prior experience.
We therefore designed Study 3 to improve our understanding of what specific kinds of experiences people might have meant to convey when they reported a "blank mind."
To do so, we separated the mind-blanking phenomenon into two separate and more specific thought report categories, within subjects, to assess their respective reporting rates.
Studies 1a and 1b received ethics approval from the UNC Greensboro Institutional Review Board (IRB; protocol number 23-278).

The methods for Studies 1a and 1b were identical except that Study 1b had a larger participant sample and a longer SART to reduce on-task report rates observed in Study 1a (Ms ≈ .75), and to potentially increase the low mind-blanking rates from Study 1a.

As stated in our preregistrations (https://osf.io/kxgqy/), we conducted a sensitivity analysis using G*Power for Study 1a ("Mind Blanking Exploratory Online Study") based on our resources for paying subjects.

text.text: A t-test comparing pairwise independent means with 150 subjects in each thought-probe-type condition (N = 450 across three conditions) yields 80% power (alpha = .05) for effect size d = 0.32, 90% power for d = 0.38, and 95% power for d = 0.42.
We preregistered a larger sample for Study 1b ("Mind Blanking Exploratory Online Study, Follow-Up Study 2").

A sensitivity analysis for a t-test comparing pairwise independent means indicated that 250 subjects in each of the 3 conditions (N = 750 total) yields 80% power for d = .25, 90% power for d = .29, and 95% power for d = .32.
Four hundred seventy-one subjects completed Study 1a and 786 completed Study 1b via the online recruitment site, Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/).

text.text: The study could only be completed on a desktop or laptop computer.
Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for any animal name and to withhold responses ("no-go") for any crop (fruit or vegetable) name; animal names occurred on 90% of the task trials.
All words were centrally presented onscreen for 272 ms followed by a pattern mask (XXXXXXXXXXXX) for 1224 ms.
Subjects could press the spacebar during the presentation of either the word or the mask to record their responses.
Before the start of the task, subjects completed ten practice trials with boy names ("go") and girl names ("no-go").
For Study 1a, subjects completed 480 critical trials divided into four seamless blocks of 120 (16 unanalyzed buffer trials preceded the critical trials).
The full stimulus list included 144 unique animal names and 16 crop names.
For Study 1b, two additional trial blocks were added to the SART, for a total of 720 critical trials.
The stimulus list for Study 1b included 214 unique animal names and 24 crop names.
In both experiments, each stimulus was pseudo-randomly presented three times per block; all stimuli were presented in the same order to all subjects.
Each block also presented six thought probes to capture subjects' immediately preceding thoughts; these were randomized and then presented in the same order to everyone.
Each thought-probe screen presented the following: "What were you just thinking about?
Please press a number on the keyboard," with the probe response options appearing below.

Six probe options were consistent across all experimental conditions; italicized text below represents the verbatim descriptions from the on-screen instructions (response options that differed across conditions will be discussed subsequently): 1.
The task/task performance ("If you were thinking about the computer task, or about how you are doing on it.") ; 2.

Everyday things/personal worries ("Select this if your thoughts were about normal, routine things you did recently or that you'll be doing later, or about big or small life concerns or worries.") ; 3.

Current state of being ("Select this if you were thinking about your state of mind or feelings, such as thinking about being sleepy, Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 18 cheerful, hungry, curious, or bored.") ; 4.
Daydreams/fantasies ("Select this for fantasies or thoughts disconnected from reality, like thoughts about flying, or being at the beach.") ; 5.
External environment ("Select this if you were thinking about something in your environment, other than the task, like sights or sounds in the room.").
"Other" was also an option for all conditions, for thoughts that did not fall into any other provided categories ("Select 'other'' ONLY if your thoughts don't fit the other options.").
Additional thought responses were dependent on experimental conditions, described below.
The task instructions presented a description of each thought-probe option before the start of SART.
Each probe remained onscreen for 10 s, regardless of when or whether the participant answered.
Study 1a presented 24 probes and Study 1b presented 36.

The Gorilla program randomly assigned subjects to one of three conditions that differed in thought probe response-menu options (see Figure 1); italicized text again represents the verbatim descriptions from the on-screen instructions.

text.text: The MB but no IDK condition included a mind-blanking ("blank mind") response option (#6; "You were not thinking about the task or anything else at all-Your mind was a complete blank."), and each probe response was followed by a confidence rating screen.

The confidence screen asked subjects to rate their confidence in their thought-report choice on a 1-5 scale, with the following labels, 1 ("not at all confident"), 2 ("somewhat confident"), 3 ("confident"), 4 ("very confident"), 5 ("extremely confident").
We included confidence ratings for only this condition because the "I-don't-know" response option in other conditions (see below) served the role of capturing low-confidence responses.

The MB & IDK condition included both a "blank mind" option (#6) and a "don't know/can't report" option (#8; "If you don't know or can't recollect what your immediately preceding thoughts were Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 19 about").

text.text: Finally, the IDK but no MB condition had a "don't know/can't report" (#7) option but no "blank mind" option.

text.text: After consenting to participate, subjects answered two simple free-response questions to filter out bots and extremely inattentive subjects.
If subjects answered at least one question correctly, they proceeded to a demographics survey that inquired about their gender, age, birth year, race/ethnicity, and highest level of education.
Then, they were informed about the purpose of our study and instructed to switch off their phones:
This study is about attention.

To ensure subjects read and understood the instructions of the SART with animal (go) and crop (no-go) stimuli, they had to first answer the following comprehension question: "When performing this task, which words should you NOT press any key for?"

text.text: As a non-preregistered exploratory analysis, we examined the correlation between confidence ratings and mind-blanking rates to investigate whether subjects with fewer mindblanking experiences were less confident in their blanking reports and vice versa.

We preregistered for a different correlational analysis that we would report both Kendall's tau and Pearson's product-moment correlations because the skewness for the mind-blanking rates for Study 1a and Study 1b were 5.346 (SE = 0.139) and 4.380 (SE = 0.108), respectively, making tau more appropriate.
In the interest of space, however, we will only report Pearson's correlations when their statistical significance differs from tau's.
In Study 1a, tau was not significant, τ(56) = .17, p = 0.101, but the Pearson's correlation was, r(56) = .30, [.05, .52], p = 0.021.
The correlation was not significant in Study 1b, with a larger sample, τ(105) = .06, p = 0.423.

We hypothesized that mind-blanking reports reflect, at least sometimes or in part, instances where people have difficulty remembering or accessing their immediately preceding thought content or experiences.

If true, then mind-blanking reports should be made with longer RTs than other varieties of off-task reports, perhaps with similar latencies as I-don't-know reports that also reflect uncertainty (note that we only preregistered this analysis for Study 2, after completing Studies 1a and 1b).

text.text: We conducted pairwise comparisons via withinperson paired t-tests (with Holm corrections for multiple comparisons) to compare probe RTs between mind-blanking reports and those for other thought categories to examine whether subjects were especially slow to report mind-blanking.
Note that these RT analyses, here and across all our subsequent experiments, should be interpreted cautiously because many subjects had very few observations for each thought type.
Table 4 presents the statistical details for the comparison of interest.
In Study 1a, mind-blanking RTs were significantly longer than those from only on-task reports (see Table 4).
On-task RTs were significantly shorter than every other thought category, except for I-don't-know reports (in Study 1a), likely due to few observations for the latter.

Mindblanking report RTs and I-don't-know report RTs were not statistically different from one another in Study 1a or Study 1b, although mean RTs were 440 and 640 ms shorter, respectively, for mind-blanking than I-don't-know reports.

Contrary to our hypothesis, however, mindblanking reports were not significantly slower than other task-unrelated thought reports, and BFs did not indicate modest evidence for either the null or alternative hypotheses.

The lack of Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 33 significant RT differences here challenges our hypothesis that subjects reporting mind-blanking would initially attempt to retrieve an experience but, failing that, would make a delayed "blanking" report that reflected failed meta-consciousness or uncertainty.
Instead, it appears that subjects readily apprehended and reported a state of having no thoughts or experience.

We evaluated whether subjects were accepting or skeptical of mind-blanking experiences.

In Study 1a, the post-SART exploratory question indicated that 68.5% of subjects (n = 308 in the two probe conditions with a mind-blanking response option) reported that the mindblanking phenomenon "makes sense" to them and they believe they have experienced it in everyday life; an additional 24.3% indicated that the phenomenon "makes sense" to them, whether or not they had experienced it.
Only 7.1% of subjects indicated that mind-blanking doesn't make sense to them and that they're skeptical that others experience it.
(As noted earlier, we were unable to collect data for this question in Study 1b due to a programming error.)
Most subjects were reportedly accepting of the mind-blanking phenomenon.

Studies 1a and 1b examined the construct validity of mind-blanking reports using different probe response options across three conditions.
Both studies indicated that, on average, adults experience mind-blanking infrequently in an online-experiment context.

The mind-blanking rates here (M rates ≈ .05) were generally a bit lower than those from prior laboratory studies (typical Ms = .10-.15; e.g., Andrillon et al., 2021; Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024; Ward & Wegner, 2013), perhaps due to the online setting or participant sample (or both).
